extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate discrete mathematics students and instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Classroom-tested worksheets and instructor notes for exploring polyhedra, Euler’s formula, Poincaré’s formula (higher genus surfaces), Towers of Hanoi constructions, and related discrete-math projects. Exercises require computing V,E,F, angle deficiencies, genera, constructing graphs, and producing proofs by induction/graph-theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle deficiency at a vertex
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle deficiency at a vertex of a polyhedron P is the sum of the angles at the corners of the faces that meet at that vertex subtracted from 2π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to compute the per-vertex deficiency: angle_deficiency(vi) = 2π - (sum of face corner angles at vi). The worksheets use this per-vertex number when filling tables for Platonic and Archimedean solids, and when summing to obtain the total angle deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total angle deficiency of a convex polyhedron
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture (and derived result): the total angle deficiency of a convex polyhedron P equals 4π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive by summing angle deficiencies over all vertices and equating that to sums over faces; use the fact that the sum of angles in each face fj is (nfj - 2)π, that Σ_j nfj = 2E, and apply Euler’s theorem (V - E + F = 2). The worksheet walks through (a) sum of angles around vertices equals sum of angles in faces, (b) sum of angles in an n-gon is (n-2)π, (c) Σ nfj = 2E, then combines these to conclude total deficiency = 4π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of interior angles of a convex n-gon
rubrics_metrics.description: The sum of the interior angles in a convex n-gon equals (n − 2)π (or 180(n−2) degrees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction: base case a triangle (n=3); if you draw a diagonal you split an n-gon into smaller polygons and apply induction. Use this fact to compute angles of regular n-gons (single angle = (n−2)π / n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of vertex-angle sum and face-angle sum
rubrics_metrics.description: The total measure of all corner angles of a polyhedron equals both Σ_{i=1}^V (sum of angles around vertex v_i) and Σ_{j=1}^F (sum of angles in face f_j).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that both sums count the same set of corner angles (once grouped by vertex, once by face). This equality is used as step (a) in the derivation of total angle deficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each face's number of sides counted equals twice the edges
rubrics_metrics.description: Σ_{j=1}^F n_{f_j} = 2E, where n_{f_j} is the number of sides of face f_j and E is the total number of edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each edge belongs to two faces (or is counted twice when summing face side counts). The worksheets use this fact as step (c) in the angle-deficiency/Euler derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Euler’s theorem (genus 0) for polyhedra
rubrics_metrics.description: For polyhedra homeomorphic to the sphere, V − E + F = 2 (Euler characteristic = 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Euler’s theorem when simplifying sums involving V, E, F to compute total angle deficiency and other global invariants. The worksheet explicitly uses Euler’s theorem in the derivation that total angle deficiency = 4π.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré’s formula and genus counting
rubrics_metrics.description: For surfaces constructed from polyhedral pieces, the Euler characteristic χ = V − E + F changes with genus; for an n-holed torus (genus n) the relation used is χ = 2 − 2n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises guide students to construct polyhedral tori (a torus, two-holed torus, etc.), count vertices/edges/faces (noting removed glued faces), compute V − E + F, and thereby determine genus. Use Poincaré’s formula to check intuition about number of holes; example: a single torus template yields χ = 0, a two-holed torus χ = −2, and in general χ = 2 − 2n for n-holed torus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting changes under gluing (constructing higher-genus polyhedra)
rubrics_metrics.description: When gluing polyhedral pieces along faces, properly account for removed faces, identified edges, and vertices when counting V,E,F for the glued surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet instructs: when gluing tori, remove entirely one face of each torus to glue them together and adjust counts accordingly (remove faces, identify shared edges/vertices). Examples compute V,E,F for 1-, 2-, 3-holed tori and show how to combine counts to predict general formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting holes/genus from modified solids (punched cube example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine genus by counting V,E,F of a modified solid (e.g., cube with square holes) and applying Poincaré’s formula to compute genus (g = (2 − χ)/2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worksheet gives the punched-cube example: subdivide faces, cut square holes through opposing middle squares, then count resulting vertices/edges/faces (ensuring faces themselves are not counted if they have holes), compute χ and solve for genus. The example concludes genus 5 and connects to Menger Sponge construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping Towers of Hanoi solutions to Hamiltonian paths
rubrics_metrics.description: The optimal solution sequence of the n-disk Towers of Hanoi corresponds to a Hamiltonian path on the n-dimensional hypercube (or to a Hamiltonian path on the Hanoi graph H_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding rule: label disks 0..n−1; each digit i in the move sequence corresponds to movement in the i-th coordinate direction of the n-cube. For the ternary-state Hanoi graph H_n (vertices = 3^n ternary strings), adjacency corresponds to legal single-disk moves; existence of a Hamiltonian path that visits all vertices gives a method to obtain a solution from any legal configuration. Exercises ask students to trace the path for n=3,4 and generalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: State encoding (Code of Hanoi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Encode a Hanoi configuration as a ternary string p_n...p_0 where p_i ∈ {0,1,2} is the peg number of disk i; conversely, decode a state to determine the physical configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for legal next states: disk 0 can always move to either of the other two pegs; except for positions with all disks on one peg, there will be exactly one other movable disk—the smallest disk not on same peg as disk 0. Use this to list successor states without drawing the full configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and adjacency rule for the Hanoi graph H_n
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct H_n by arranging the 3^n ternary-labeled vertices in a triangular recursive layout (append 0 to H_{n−1}, add 1 modulo 3 and rotate, add 2 modulo 3 and rotate) and insert edges where two states are mutually obtainable by a single legal move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The worksheet specifies the recursive placement and rotation depending on parity of n (rotate 120° clockwise or counterclockwise). Edges are drawn between vertices whose states are attainable from one another by one legal disk move. Exercises: draw H1..H3 and find Hamiltonian paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ternary-sum algorithm for kth position of Hanoi
rubrics_metrics.description: Given k (written in binary b_{n−1}...b_0) and n, determine the state after k moves by forming a specific list of ternary strings (patterns differ for n even/odd), and adding them column-wise modulo 3 (without carrying) to obtain the ternary state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives explicit rows to sum (one per binary digit) with different pattern rows depending on parity of n; example provided for k=141, n=8. Exercises ask students to apply algorithm to compute states after given k and identify which disk moved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-colorability of line maps (proof methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any line map (finite collection of infinite straight lines dividing the plane) can be two-colored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proof methods are given: (1) induction on number of lines: remove a line, two-color the resulting map, then put the line back and reverse colors on one side to maintain alternation; (2) parity/right-side count: orient each line, for each region count the number of lines it is on the 'right' side of, color by parity of that count. Exercises ask students to produce both proofs and compare them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-colorability of closed-curve maps (proof methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any closed-curve map (single closed curve possibly with self-intersections, in general position) can be two-colored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two proof approaches: (1) induction on number of crossings using smoothing (show that smoothing preserves two-colorability and one can choose a smoothing leaving the curve connected); (2) graph-theory approach by taking the dual graph of regions and showing all faces of the dual have even length (hence the dual is bipartite), then two-coloring vertices of dual corresponds to two-coloring regions. Exercises walk through smoothing argument and graph dual construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting perfect matchings in benzenoids (method prerequisites)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count perfect matchings in certain hexagonal systems (benzenoids), apply combinatorial and determinant-based methods requiring familiarity with counting techniques, graphs, and determinants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor notes indicate students should be familiar with counting principles, graph theory, and determinants. The article describes several efficient counting methods for special classes of graphs and mentions implementing a general determinant-based formula; exercises and references are provided for further study.
